item.title: Monte Carlo-based secondary dose check platform for the world's first ultra-compact upright proton therapy system
item.description: arXiv:2611.33924v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Objective. This work aimed to develop and validate an independent Monte Carlo (MC) secondary dose check of the RayStation treatment planning system (TPS) for the Mevion S250-FIT, the world's first ultra-compact upright proton therapy system. Approach. The treatment nozzle, including the energy modulation system of boron carbide and polycarbonate plates and the adaptive aperture, was modeled in the TOPAS (TOol for PArticle Simulation) MC code, and the beam model was commissioned against integrated depth dose curves, in-air spot profiles, and dose per monitor unit measured at 12 energy settings. Based on this model, an in-house converter, RayStation2TOPAS, recalculates the TPS plans by reconstructing each pencil beam spot, the aperture for each energy layer, and the seated patient's rotation. In total, 15 water phantom plans and 25 clinical plans were recalculated and compared with the TPS by the point dose, with a tolerance of 5%, and by three-dimensional gamma analysis at 3%/2mm, with a pass rate of at least 90%. Main results. The simulated proton range agreed with the measurement within 0.25mm, the spot full width at half maximum within 6.8%, and the dose per monitor unit within 1.3%. The point dose differed from the TPS by -0.76% to +1.98% in the water phantom plans and by -3.03% to +3.99% in the clinical plans, with gamma pass rates of 96.39% to 99.93% and 90.08% to 99.98%, so every plan passed both tests. Significance. To our knowledge, this is the first independent MC secondary dose check for the S250-FIT, and it complements measurement-based patient-specific quality assurance of its plans.

item.title: DosePET: An Open-Source Dataset with 2100 Radiation Dose Maps for PET/CT
item.description: arXiv:2611.34008v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large collections of three-dimensional radiation dose maps linked to patient anatomy are needed to develop artificial intelligence (AI) models for personalized internal dosimetry in nuclear medicine, but access to such data remains limited. Here we present DosePET, an open-source dataset of 2,100 patient-specific absorbed-dose maps generated by Monte Carlo simulation of publicly available PET/CT examinations: 1,503 [18F]FDG examinations from ENHANCE.PET and 369 [18F]PSMA-1007 and 228 [68Ga]Ga-PSMA-11 examinations from PSMA-PET-CT-Lesions, acquired at five institutions with seven scanner models. For each examination, the CT was resampled to the native PET grid to build a voxelized patient phantom, the quantitative PET image defined the radionuclide source, and radiation transport was simulated with GATE version 9.4. Organ and tissue masks were generated from the CT with TotalSegmentator. Each study folder contains a NIfTI dose map integrated from scan time to infinity, 117 binary organ/tissue masks, a report of regional dosimetric quantities, including mean absorbed doses, dose conversion factors and scan-time dose rates, and simulation metadata. The total processing time was 1,542.4 hours. Python tools support selective downloading and conversion to scan-time dose-rate or dose-per-decay maps, and an agent skill guides pairing with the source PET/CT images. DosePET is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/eltzanis/DosePET.
item.dc:creator: Eleftherios Tzanis, Antonios Tzortzakakis, Michail E. Klontzas

item.title: Fewer Fractions, Equieffective Plans: An optimization framework based on equieffective dose
item.description: arXiv:2611.34605v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Background: Non-standard fractionation requires caution before clinical use, and planners often need to manually modify the prescription and dose constraints for non-linear biological effects. Purpose: To develop an extension within a treatment planning system that enables the generation of hypofractionated plans based on equieffective dose, $EQD_{n_{ref}}$, for an alternative fractionation deliverable in $n$ fractions, such that it is equieffective with the reference fractionation for a specified biological endpoint. Methods: A research build of RayStation v2025 was extended to optimize $EQD_{n_{ref}}$ plans. This study used anonymized data from three head and neck patients. $\text{CTV}_p$ and $\text{CTV}_n$ were prescribed 70 Gy and 54 Gy in 35 fractions. Targets, spinal cord, and brainstem were robustly optimized for $\pm3.5$% density and $\pm3.0$ mm setup uncertainties. For each patient, hypofractionated plans were created with 34, 32, 30, and 25 fractions. Sensitivity analysis evaluated the impact of $\alpha/\beta$ uncertainty. Results: All equieffective hypofractionated plans maintained target coverage and met mandatory clinical goals for organs-at-risk (OARs). Compared to standard fractionation, DVH parameters indicated an average $\Delta EQD_{n_{ref}}$ <0.2 Gy for $\text{CTV}_p$ and no difference for $\text{CTV}_n$. For parallel OARs, the median mean-dose difference between hypofractionation (to 30 fractions) and standard fractionation was generally <1% of the prescribed dose. $\alpha/\beta$ uncertainty produced the greatest variation in the 25-fraction regimen, with absolute $\Delta EQD_{n_{ref}}$ up to 0.88 Gy for targets and up to 0.63 Gy for the spinal cord and brainstem. Conclusions: An $EQD_{n_{ref}}$-based framework can generate equieffective hypofractionated plans, making it feasible to reduce fractions without substantially deviating from existing clinical protocols.
item.dc:creator: Suryakant Kaushik, Jakob \"Od\'en, Albin Fredriksson, Iuliana Toma-Dasu

item.title: Do Not Let the Prior Heal the Anomaly: Selective Anchoring for Detection from Incomplete Measurements
item.description: arXiv:2611.33331v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generative priors can recover anatomical detail from incomplete medical measurements, but may erase the very lesions that imaging aims to detect, even when the measurements contain evidence of them. We introduce selective anchoring that protects reliably measured image components from prior-driven changes, while allowing expressive generative models to reconstruct unresolved structure. Acquisition uncertainty in the protected components is either added deterministically to the downstream test or carried by the ensemble through stochastic perturbations of the readings. We implement this principle as a wrapper for pretrained diffusion and flow samplers and as AnchoredFM, a fast constrained flow model. Under a linear-Gaussian measurement model, the protected coefficients are unbiased in expectation and achieve nominal interval coverage across repeated acquisitions, independently of the learned prior. Across sparse-view CT, accelerated brain MRI, and photoacoustic tomography, selective anchoring improves lesion contrast preservation and uncertainty reliability, and can reduce reconstruction error within lesions. For tumor detection in accelerated MRI, with a healthy reference estimated from the measurements alone, deterministic anchoring raises mean AUROC across eight samplers from 78.4% to 84.6% and lesion sensitivity at 0.25 false-positive marks per slice from 38.8% to 47.5%, with gains in all four predefined tumor-size groups. At thresholds frozen on healthy validation data, mean sensitivity rises from 20.2% to 44.1% (37.6% with stochastic anchoring). These findings show how expressive generative priors can reconstruct unresolved anatomy without healing away the abnormalities that the measurements support.
item.dc:creator: Nicolas Tricard, Stefan Brandst\"atter, Jason Chen, Zituo Chen, Linzheng Wang, Georg Langs, Sili Deng

item.title: Liver Lesion Detection with Task-Specific Organ-Level Tube Current Modulation: A Retrospective Reader Study
item.description: arXiv:2607.25440v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Rationale and Objectives: To evaluate whether task-specific organ-level TCM improves hepatic lesion detection and abdominal image quality compared with uniform dose reduction at equivalent effective dose. Materials and Methods: In this single-center, IRB-approved, retrospective study, 22 oncology patients with 68 liver lesions (38 malignant, 30 benign) underwent chest-abdomen-pelvis CT. Using projection-domain noise emulation, five series were generated per patient: original acquisition (Orig-100); uniform reduction to 40% (UD-40) and 60% (UD-60) of effective dose; and organ-level TCM at matched 40% (Opt-40) and 60% (Opt-60). Three abdominal radiologists independently detected and classified lesions as benign or malignant and rated image quality on a 5-point Likert scale. Per-lesion sensitivity and image-quality scores were compared using the McNemar and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, respectively. Malignant lesion-size thresholds (x50, x90) were estimated by logistic regression. Results: At 60% dose, Opt-60 malignant sensitivity was comparable to Orig-100 (82% vs 80%) and higher than UD-60 (67%). At 40% dose, Opt-40 exceeded UD-40 (68% vs 52%). All lesion detection improved similarly (Opt vs UD: 64% vs 54% at 40%; 77% vs 65% at 60%), with Opt-60 comparable to full dose (77% vs 76%). All Opt-versus-UD detection differences were significant (p <= 0.003). Opt-60 lesion-size thresholds (x50 = 3.3 mm; x90 = 15.7 mm) matched Orig-100 (3.7 mm, 16.8 mm). Abdominal image quality was higher with Opt than UD at both doses. Conclusion: At equivalent effective dose, organ-level TCM improved liver lesion detection over uniform reduction, with Opt-60 comparable to full dose. These findings support organ-level optimization for dose reduction while preferentially preserving image quality for liver metastasis detection.
